_meta: A one-dimensional texture and a minification factor, used to show that drawing a texture smaller than its resolution requires sampling from a PREFILTERED mip level chosen by the minification, not point-sampling the full-resolution texture -- and that picking the wrong level either aliases (too low) or over-blurs (too high). A mipmap is a precomputed pyramid: level 0 is the texture, level 1 is level 0 with every 2x2 block (here every pair) averaged to half the size, level 2 halves again, and so on, so each level is a correctly prefiltered smaller copy. When a textured surface is minified so that each screen pixel covers m texels, point-sampling level 0 reads one texel per screen pixel and skips the other m-1, which aliases: the sampled values are not the average of the region the pixel covers, so fine detail turns into a false pattern and shimmers when the view moves. The fix is to sample the level whose texels are about one screen pixel wide, which is level log2(m): at that level each texel already holds the average of the m original texels the screen pixel covers, so the sample is the true footprint average. Sampling a level higher than that reads a texel averaging more originals than the pixel covers, so neighboring pixels that should differ collapse to the same value -- over-blur. On this fixture the texture is a 16-texel ramp and the minification is 4, so each screen pixel covers 4 texels, the correct level is 2, and the true footprint averages are 15, 55, 95, 135; level 0 point-sampling gives 0, 40, 80, 120 (aliased low), level 2 gives exactly the footprint averages, and level 3 gives 35, 35, 115, 115 (adjacent pixels collapsed). The texture and the minification factor are the fixture; the mip pyramid, the footprint averages, and the samples at each level are computed. Stdlib only.
